introduction: Bahá’u’lláh addressed the kings of His day directly, and what He said to them is the first matter of this guide: you hold the reins of government in trust, “that ye may rule with justice,” protect the downtrodden, and not burden your people to build palaces. A just king has “a great station.” He adds two things that look forward. A republic profits all, yet “the majesty of kingship is one of the signs of God,” and the best arrangement joins the two, as in a constitutional monarchy; and a sign of the world’s maturity is that no one will be willing to bear the weight of kingship alone. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s letters apply this to Persia’s struggle for a constitution. The last readings set all earthly crowns beside “an eternal Kingdom” and picture kings coming on foot to the Shrines. Deuteronomy’s law for kings, Samuel’s and David’s words, the Psalms, Sa‘dí, Confucius and Mencius describe the same just ruler; Montesquieu, Acton, Locke and Kant belong with the constitutional readings; Shelley, Gray, Khayyám and Kipling with those on passing glory. Samuel’s warning against having a king at all, Paine’s “necessary evil,” and Machiavelli’s “safer to be feared than loved” are the dissent.
questions: “Your people are your treasures.” What would change in any institution you know if those who lead it believed this?
Bahá’u’lláh praises both republican government and “the majesty of kingship.” What does each contribute, and what does a constitutional monarchy keep of both?
“No one will accept to bear alone the weight of kingship.” Why is shared responsibility a sign of maturity?
Believers are told to obey their governments; a tyrant is said to forfeit his right to rule; David would not strike Saul. How do you hold these together?
The poets say that every crown ends in dust, and the last readings speak of a sovereignty that does not. What is the “sovereignty of service,” and who has had it?

outside.why: “God hath committed into your hands the reins of the government of the people, that ye may rule with justice.” David’s last words: he that ruleth over men must be just, ruling in the fear of God.
To “safeguard the rights of the downtrodden.” The psalm for a king: he shall judge thy people with righteousness, and thy poor with judgment.

“Thou art God’s shadow on earth.” Shakespeare’s Claudius, a murderer and usurper, relies on the same idea: there’s such divinity doth hedge a king, that treason can but peep to what it would. What must be true of a king, on the reading’s terms, for the title to mean anything?
“Your people are your treasures.” Sa‘dí told the Persian court the same: the sheep is not for the shepherd, but the shepherd for the service of the sheep.
“Do not rob them to rear palaces for yourselves.” Jeremiah to a king of Judah: woe unto him that buildeth his house by unrighteousness, and his chambers by wrong.

“Lay not excessive burdens on your peoples.” Rehoboam, asked to lighten the yoke, answered that he would add to it, and lost ten tribes: my father chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions.
Kings manifest divine power, “and what is intended is their justice.” Proverbs: mercy and truth preserve the king: and his throne is upholden by mercy.
The ancient kings of Persia are remembered with approval. Isaiah gives one of them a title he gives no other foreign ruler: thus saith the Lord to his anointed, to Cyrus.
A prayer that the sovereign may protect “His flock … from the wolves of the earth.” Ezekiel on the shepherd-king: I will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which was sick.

“The just king is the lamp of the world.” Confucius: he who exercises government by means of his virtue may be compared to the north polar star, which keeps its place and all the stars turn towards it.

The just king is “as the head to the body.” Mencius ranks them the other way round: the people are the most important element in a nation; the sovereign is the lightest. Both sayings agree that the king exists for the people.

“The majesty of kingship is one of the signs of God.” Samuel thought Israel’s wish for a king a rejection of God, and warned what a king would cost: he will take your sons, and appoint them for himself, for his chariots, and to be his horsemen. How do the readings answer Samuel’s warning?

A republic “profits all the people,” yet kingship should not be lost. Thomas Paine, in the year of American independence: government even in its best state is but a necessary evil. What does Bahá’u’lláh see in kingship that Paine does not?

A sign of the world’s maturity: “no one will accept to bear alone the weight of kingship.” Plato: the State in which the rulers are most reluctant to govern is always the best and most quietly governed.
Shakespeare’s Henry IV, sleepless while his poorest subjects sleep, says why a king might wish the weight shared: uneasy lies the head that wears a crown.

Vast countries should not be governed from a single centre. Jethro to Moses, who was judging every case himself: the thing that thou doest is not good; this thing is too heavy for thee; thou art not able to perform it thyself alone.
Government and nation should “blend together like milk and honey.” Proverbs: where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.

“Consider how powerful … the constitutional government of England is.” Montesquieu drew his principle from the same example: when the legislative and executive powers are united in the same person, there can be no liberty.

A king under law. Deuteronomy required it of Israel’s kings: he shall write him a copy of this law in a book, and he shall read therein all the days of his life: that his heart be not lifted up above his brethren.
“It is impossible that a despotic government could make any progress.” Lord Acton: power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely.

A sultan is advised to give “complete freedom of rights to all thy subjects no matter to what religion they may belong.” The emperor Ashoka had cut such a rule in stone: whoever praises his own religion and condemns others only harms his own religion.

Each country may have its head, “but there will not be a supreme king for the whole world.” Kant, planning perpetual peace, preferred a federation to the fusion of all the States into a Universal Monarchy by one Power.
“Pray ye on their behalf.” Paul: supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, for kings, and for all that are in authority.
God “hath committed the world and the cities thereof to the care of the kings.” Paul: the powers that be are ordained of God.

The kingdom is in God’s hand; “He bestoweth it upon whomsoever He pleaseth.” The Qur’án: O Allah! Owner of Sovereignty! Thou givest sovereignty unto whom Thou wilt, and Thou withdrawest sovereignty from whom Thou wilt.
“Blessed be the king whose sovereignty hath withheld him not from his Sovereign.” The psalm: be wise now therefore, O ye kings. Serve the Lord with fear.
“Be submissive to all monarchs that are just.” Peter: fear God. Honour the king.
A tyrant “forfeits the right to govern.” Locke: whenever the legislators endeavour to reduce the people to slavery under arbitrary power, they put themselves into a state of war with the people.

David had Saul, who was hunting him, at his mercy in a cave, and would not strike: I will not put forth mine hand against my lord; for he is the Lord’s anointed. How do you weigh his restraint beside this reading and beside the readings on obedience that follow?
“That which is necessary today is obedience to government.” Jesus: render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s.
The order of countries and “the security of paths” depend on government. Proverbs: the king by judgment establisheth the land.
“All these matters arise from the weakness of the government.” Ecclesiastes: woe to thee, O land, when thy king is a child.
Kingship protects, but “it should go hand in hand with Justice.” Pascal: justice without might is helpless; might without justice is tyrannical.
A prayer for the monarch’s safety. Israel at its first coronation: all the people shouted, and said, God save the king.
A queen goes daily to church and is called heedless. Jesus: not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord.
Glory was taken from two kings, as foretold. Daniel: he removeth kings, and setteth up kings.
“You will see the name of the Qajar obliterated.” The writing on Belshazzar’s wall: God hath numbered thy kingdom, and finished it.
“Crowns and thrones were overturned.” Mary’s song: he hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree.

Kings once could give peace or make war at will. Machiavelli advised them on keeping such power: it is much safer to be feared than loved. What became of rulers who followed him, on the evidence of these readings?
People will turn on the statesmen who sent them to war. Isaiah’s taunt over a fallen king: how art thou fallen from heaven! how art thou cut down to the ground, which didst weaken the nations!
“Today the true duty of a powerful king is to establish a universal peace.” Isaiah: the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called The Prince of Peace.
Kings should “lay fast hold on religion.” Solomon’s prayer at his accession: give therefore thy servant an understanding heart to judge thy people.
“No king is ever at peace for a moment.” Henry V, in disguise among his soldiers: I think the king is but a man, as I am; his ceremonies laid by, in his nakedness he appears but a man.
“An eternal Kingdom … greater than that of” any emperor. Jesus before Pilate: my kingdom is not of this world.

“The Kayanian kings possessed crowns and diadems … but what benefit was it? It did not endure.” Omar Khayyám on the same kings: they say the Lion and the Lizard keep the courts where Jamshyd gloried and drank deep.
“Crowned monarchs … became bedfellows with dust.” Shelley: “My name is Ozymandias, king of kings: look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair!” Nothing beside remains.

Napoleon’s sovereignty ended with his life; Christ’s did not. John: when Jesus perceived that they would come and take him by force, to make him a king, he departed again into a mountain himself alone.
Their glory “is but temporal.” Gray: the boast of heraldry, the pomp of pow’r, awaits alike th’ inevitable hour. The paths of glory lead but to the grave.
“That which ye possess shall perish in less than a moment.” Kipling, at the height of an empire: lo, all our pomp of yesterday is one with Nineveh and Tyre!
“If thou seekest royal grandeur … seek servitude.” Jesus: whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister.
“The true sovereigns … are the servants.” Laozi on why rivers and seas are kings of the valleys: their skill in being lower than they.
“Become a sovereign in the kingdom of mystic knowledge.” Plato’s hope for cities: until philosophers are kings, or the kings and princes of this world have the spirit and power of philosophy.
A vision of monarchs laying down their crowns and coming on foot to the Shrines. The psalm: yea, all kings shall fall down before him: all nations shall serve him.
Isaiah: the Gentiles shall come to thy light, and kings to the brightness of thy rising.
John’s city: the kings of the earth do bring their glory and honour into it.
Kings will disembark and come “on foot and bareheaded.” The wise men at Bethlehem: they fell down, and worshipped him: and when they had opened their treasures, they presented unto him gifts.

shortfall: A large share of the 76 readings are prayers and good wishes for particular rulers of Persia, Turkey and Britain, or brief remarks on events of the time, and many repeat the same praise of just kingship. The guide is read with 56 outside quotations, placed where they add a parallel, a test or an objection; none was added only to reach the number of 81.

psalm-all-kings-shall-fall-down.text: The kings of Tarshish and of the isles shall bring presents: the kings of Sheba and Seba shall offer gifts. Yea, all kings shall fall down before him: all nations shall serve him

isaiah-kings-shall-be-thy-nursing-father.text: And kings shall be thy nursing fathers, and their queens thy nursing mothers: they shall bow down to thee with their face toward the earth, and lick up the dust of thy feet; and thou shalt know that I am the Lord: for they shall not be ashamed that wait for me

quran-kings-when-they-enter-a-township.text: She said: Lo! kings, when they enter a township, ruin it and make the honour of its people shame. Thus will they do.

kings-my-father-chastised-you-with-whips.text: And the king answered the people roughly, and forsook the old men's counsel that they gave him; And spake to them after the counsel of the young men, saying, My father made your yoke heavy, and I will add to your yoke: my father also chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions
